new_statements.rule_in_words: Denya is described as a register-tone language (H, L, rising, falling, downstepped H); none of the three accessible descriptions makes any statement about word stress, its position, or its absence. No rule for stress placement can be stated from an opened source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement to have exceptions).
new_statements.domain_note: Mbuagbaw 2002 is a noun-class morphology article by the language's principal describer (CABTAL) with a one-page phonological overview; the tone statement is lexical/word-level (examples are nouns with prefix tones). Bakume 2005 is a comparative D.E.A. thesis whose Denya sketch is of the Takamanda (reference) dialect. Neither is the full phonology (Mbuagbaw 1996/1999), which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Mbuagbaw 2002 treats Denya as a whole (four dialects: Takamanda, Basho, Betieku, Bajwa; data from a CABTAL language committee). Bakume 2005's phonology sketch is explicitly of the Takamanda reference dialect. Glottolog 5.3 lists deny1238 with alternative names Anyang/Anyah/Nyang/Takamanda/Obonya and no dialect-level glottocodes on the page downloaded. Abangma 1992 calls the language 'Ekoid Bantu'; Mbuagbaw 2002 places it in the Nyang sub-group of Southern Bantoid.

new_statements.quote: Denya is a tone language like most African languages. On the surface Denya has two level tones [ ´ ] and low [ ` ] and two contour tones falling [ ^ ] and rising [ ˇ ]. In addition there is the phenomenon of downstep high being marked /ꜜH/. […] 5.1 Tonal Phonemes In a tone language, the speaker uses the pitch of his voice to distinguish lexically between morphemes or words that would have been otherwise identical. new_statements.rule_in_words: Denya (analysis based on the Takamanda dialect; four dialects Takamanda, Basho, Bitieku, Bajwa named p. 6) is described as a tone language: level tones H and L, contour tones falling and rising, plus downstepped H; the syllable is defined as segments plus tone (§3.1/4.1); chapter 5 treats noun tone patterns (L, H, LH, HL on roots; downstep H absent on monosyllabic noun roots), associative-construction tone rules, verb tone classes (L, H, LH; disyllabic HH) and paradigms, downdrift and downstep, and contour tones (rising tones on noun-class prefixes and noun stems, never on verb roots). Word stress or accent is not mentioned anywhere in the 96 pages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: A segmental phonology of the Takamanda dialect (vowels, consonants, syllable types, segmental processes); tone is listed as a constituent of every syllable (H, L, LH, HL), verb roots carry lexical melodies (L, H, LH; disyllabic HH), semi-vowels never bear a contrastive tone, and the appendix tabulates associative-construction tone and verb tone paradigms ('Tone is an aspect of the morphology of the language'); tone analysis proper is referred to the author's 1995 tone orthography. Nothing is said about word stress or accent.

new_statements.quote: Moreover, Stem 2 (the M-verb root in the F position) has a specific tone pattern depending on whether it is mono- or disyllabic. Abangma writes: The first verb carries low tone, while the second, if monosyllabic, may have either high or low tone depending on the tone of the verb, i.e., it carries the lexical tone. A disyllabic second root morpheme carries a high tone on the first syllable and low tone on the second syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule of word stress is given anywhere in the work. Tone is lexical on verb and noun roots (H vs L monosyllabic verbs, L-H disyllabic verbs) and is manipulated by the grammar (subject concord markers change tone with verb mode; plural noun classes 2, 6, 8, 10 take a H-tone associative marker that spreads onto the preceding noun; in class 10 a H replaces the root L). The study is morphosyntactic (Fleming's stratificational model) and defers phonology to Mbuagbaw's 1994 orthography, 1995 tone orthography and 1996 phonology.
